How Item Embeddings Are Trained

One training step by hand, then the general framework: gradient descent on watch data

Son Nguyen

Where This Fits

  • In the RS lecture and practice problem, the item embeddings were given (“learned beforehand”).
  • Today: how they are learned. First one step by hand, then the general recipe.

Watched → pull the user and item vectors together. Skipped → push them apart. Repeat millions of times.

Practice Problem

Setting Up the Learning Problem

The dataset: 6 users, one row each for Podcast X.

Row User User vector \mathbf{u} Podcast Label r
1 Ann (1, 0) X 1 (listened)
2 Ben (1, 0.2) X 1 (listened)
3 Cal (1, 0.4) X 1 (listened)
4 Dee (0, 0.6) X 0 (skipped)
5 Eli (0.2, 1) X 0 (skipped)
6 Fay (0, 1) X 0 (skipped)
  • Input: a (user, podcast) pair, e.g. (Ann, X).
  • Output variable: the label r: 1 = listened, 0 = skipped.
  • Parameters: Podcast X’s embedding \mathbf{v}_X (2 numbers). The users’ vectors are given (already trained) and stay fixed here.
  • Prediction: \hat r = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}_X.
  • Loss over all 6 rows:

L(\mathbf{v}_X) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{6} \left(r_i - \mathbf{u}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}_X\right)^2

The input has no features: just two IDs. The numbers describing Podcast X are parameters, learned from the labels.

Practice Problem: Find Podcast X’s Embedding

Podcast X’s embedding starts random: \mathbf{v}_X = (0.5, 0.5). Use all 6 rows and learning rate \eta = 0.25:

e_i = r_i - \mathbf{u}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}_X, \qquad \mathbf{v}_X \leftarrow \mathbf{v}_X + \eta \sum_{i=1}^{6} e_i\, \mathbf{u}_i

(a) Compute the prediction \mathbf{u}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}_X and the error e_i for every row.

(b) Take one gradient step: update \mathbf{v}_X.

(c) Compute the new predictions and the loss before and after. Did the loss go down?

(d) If we keep repeating the step, where does \mathbf{v}_X go? Why there?

Solution (a): Predict and Find the Error for Every Row

User \mathbf{u} Label r Prediction \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}_X Error e = r - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}_X
Ann (1, 0) 1 1(0.5) + 0(0.5) = 0.5 1 - 0.5 = 0.5
Ben (1, 0.2) 1 1(0.5) + 0.2(0.5) = 0.6 1 - 0.6 = 0.4
Cal (1, 0.4) 1 1(0.5) + 0.4(0.5) = 0.7 1 - 0.7 = 0.3
Dee (0, 0.6) 0 0(0.5) + 0.6(0.5) = 0.3 0 - 0.3 = -0.3
Eli (0.2, 1) 0 0.2(0.5) + 1(0.5) = 0.6 0 - 0.6 = -0.6
Fay (0, 1) 0 0(0.5) + 1(0.5) = 0.5 0 - 0.5 = -0.5
  • Listeners (Ann, Ben, Cal): predicted too low, so the error is positive.
  • Skippers (Dee, Eli, Fay): predicted too high, so the error is negative.

Solution (b): One Gradient Step Using All 6 Users

User Error e e \times \mathbf{u}
Ann 0.5 0.5 \times (1, 0) = (0.5, 0)
Ben 0.4 0.4 \times (1, 0.2) = (0.4, 0.08)
Cal 0.3 0.3 \times (1, 0.4) = (0.3, 0.12)
Dee -0.3 -0.3 \times (0, 0.6) = (0, -0.18)
Eli -0.6 -0.6 \times (0.2, 1) = (-0.12, -0.6)
Fay -0.5 -0.5 \times (0, 1) = (0, -0.5)
Sum \mathbf{(1.08, -1.08)}

\mathbf{v}_X \leftarrow (0.5, 0.5) + 0.25 \times (1.08, -1.08) = (0.5, 0.5) + (0.27, -0.27) = \mathbf{(0.77, 0.23)}

  • Listeners (positive e) pull X toward their vectors; skippers (negative e) push it away.
  • X moved toward Ann, Ben, Cal (right) and away from Dee, Eli, Fay (up).

Solution (c): Did the Loss Go Down?

User Label r Before After: \mathbf{u}\cdot(0.77, 0.23) New error
Ann 1 0.5 1(0.77) + 0(0.23) = 0.77 0.23
Ben 1 0.6 1(0.77) + 0.2(0.23) = 0.816 0.184
Cal 1 0.7 1(0.77) + 0.4(0.23) = 0.862 0.138
Dee 0 0.3 0(0.77) + 0.6(0.23) = 0.138 -0.138
Eli 0 0.6 0.2(0.77) + 1(0.23) = 0.384 -0.384
Fay 0 0.5 0(0.77) + 1(0.23) = 0.23 -0.23

Every prediction moved toward its label: listeners up toward 1, skippers down toward 0.

L_{\text{before}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left((0.5)^2 + (0.4)^2 + (0.3)^2 + (-0.3)^2 + (-0.6)^2 + (-0.5)^2\right) = 0.6 L_{\text{after}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left((0.23)^2 + (0.184)^2 + (0.138)^2 + (-0.138)^2 + (-0.384)^2 + (-0.23)^2\right) = 0.163

The loss dropped from 0.6 to 0.16. ✓

Watch X’s Embedding Move (Click to Step Through)

Solution (d): Where Is X Heading?

Step 0 1 2 3 5 10 60
\mathbf{v}_X (0.5, 0.5) (0.77, 0.23) (0.89, 0.08) (0.95, 0) (0.99, -0.06) (1.01, -0.08) (1.01, -0.08)
  • Repeating the step, \mathbf{v}_X settles at about (1.01, -0.08): close to the listeners (all near (1, 0.2)), away from the skippers.
  • There, \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}_X \approx 1 for listeners and \approx 0 for skippers: the predictions match the labels as well as possible.
  • With the users fixed, this is linear regression: the user vectors are the features, r is the response, and \mathbf{v}_X holds the coefficients. Gradient descent reaches the least-squares answer.
  • In full training, every podcast is found this way and every user’s vector is updated by the same rule (roles swapped).

A podcast’s embedding is pulled toward the people who listened and away from those who skipped. Podcasts with the same listeners end up close together.

The General Framework

The Learning Problem in General

The dataset: 6 listeners × 6 podcasts = 36 rows

Row User Podcast Label r
1 Ann N1 1
2 Ann N2 1
3 Ann N3 1
4 Ann C1 0
5 Ann C2 0
6 Ann C3 0
7 Ben N1 1
8 Ben N2 1
9 Ben N3 0
… … … …
36 Fay C3 1

Each podcast appears in 6 rows (once per listener); each listener in 6 rows.

  • Dataset: every (user, item, label) row from the logs. Here 36 rows; at YouTube, billions.
  • Input: a (user, item) pair.
  • Output variable: r = 1 if the user watched or listened, 0 if not (sampled).
  • Parameters: a vector \mathbf{u} for every user and \mathbf{v} for every item.
  • Prediction: \hat r = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}.
  • Loss: total squared error over all rows, plus a penalty:

L = \sum_{\text{rows}} \tfrac{1}{2}\,(r - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 \;+\; \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\sum\left(\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2 + \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2\right)

  • Training: gradient descent on L, one row at a time (SGD).

From One Step to Training

start every user vector and item vector at small random numbers
repeat for many passes (epochs):
    for each (user, item, r) in the data, in random order:
        e = r − u·v
        u ← u + η·e·v          (both updates use the old u and v)
        v ← v + η·e·u
store the item vectors → used for retrieval

The Loss Behind the Rule

Training minimizes the squared error over all (user, item) pairs, plus a penalty that keeps vectors small:

L = \sum_{(\text{user},\,\text{item})} \tfrac{1}{2}\,(r - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 \;+\; \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\left(\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2 + \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2\right)

For one pair, with e = r - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}:

\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{u}} = -e\,\mathbf{v} + \lambda\mathbf{u}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{v}} = -e\,\mathbf{u} + \lambda\mathbf{v}

Step against the gradient:

\mathbf{u} \leftarrow \mathbf{u} + \eta\,(e\,\mathbf{v} - \lambda\mathbf{u}), \qquad \mathbf{v} \leftarrow \mathbf{v} + \eta\,(e\,\mathbf{u} - \lambda\mathbf{v})

  • This is gradient descent. One pair at a time = stochastic gradient descent (SGD).
  • The practice problem took one step using all 6 rows at once (batch gradient descent); SGD steps after each row. Both head to the same place. \lambda is the same ridge penalty as in regression.
  • The method is called matrix factorization: the watch table \approx (user vectors) × (item vectors).

Where the Labels Come From

Unlike a CNN, no person labels anything: behavior is the label.

Label r From the logs
1 = watched / listened Ann played Podcast X
1 = watched most of it finished more than half (filters out clickbait)
0 = not watched random items the user did not play (“negative sampling”)

A 0 is a guess: it may mean “never saw it”, not “did not want it”. Labels are free and plentiful, but noisy.

Watch It Train: 6 Listeners, 6 Podcasts (Click to Step Through)

N1 N2 N3 C1 C2 C3
Ann 1 1 1 0 0 0
Ben 1 1 0 0 0 0
Cal 0 1 1 0 0 1
Dee 0 0 0 1 1 1
Eli 0 0 0 1 1 0
Fay 1 0 0 0 1 1

1 = listened. N = news, C = comedy, but the model is not told this.

Each click = more training (SGD over all 36 cells).

What Training Achieved

  • Error: 0.45 \to 0.09 after 300 epochs.
  • News podcasts point one way, comedy another: average cosine 0.93 within a group vs 0.12 across groups.
  • The two learned numbers have no names. We only see afterward that they separate news from comedy.
  • These trained item vectors are what the RS lecture used for retrieval.

Same Recipe as Training a Neural Network

Neural network Item embeddings
Parameters weights and biases one vector per user and per item
Prediction network output \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}
Labels given (e.g. image classes) from behavior (watched = 1)
Loss squared error / cross-entropy squared error (or logistic)
Training gradient descent gradient descent (SGD)

Variations Used in Practice

Method Prediction Idea
Matrix factorization (today) \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} one free vector per user and item
Logistic version \sigma(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) = P(watch) logistic regression loss, sampled 0s
Two-tower network f(\text{user features})\cdot g(\text{item features}) neural networks make the vectors, so new items get one immediately
Item2vec items in the same session are “neighbors” like word2vec for words

All of them: predict, measure the error, step down the gradient, repeat.

After Training

  • Slow loop: item vectors are retrained on new data every day or week.
  • Fast loop: a user’s vector updates instantly from their latest plays and feedback (the Sarah practice problem).

Summary

Step In the practice problem
Data: one row per (user, podcast) with label r 6 users; Ann, Ben, Cal listened to X; Dee, Eli, Fay skipped
Start the embedding at random \mathbf{v}_X = (0.5, 0.5)
Predict \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}, error e = r - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} errors 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, -0.3, -0.6, -0.5
Gradient step: \mathbf{v} \leftarrow \mathbf{v} + \eta\sum e\,\mathbf{u} \mathbf{v}_X = (0.77, 0.23); loss 0.6 \to 0.16
Repeat (all users and items, many passes) \mathbf{v}_X \to (1.01, -0.08), near its listeners

Embeddings are learned by gradient descent from behavior: each item is pulled toward the people who used it and away from those who did not.
